Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release October 09, 2026 Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families For release at 10:00 a.m. EDT Share The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families. The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF) , which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability. Key findings from the 2025 survey include: Real median family income rose 7 percent between the 2022 to 2025 surveys to $82,200, while real mean family income fell 6 percent to $145,200. Families in the lower ends of the income and net worth distributions saw modest increases in median and mean income, while families in the upper ends saw declines. Between 2022 and 2025, real median net worth rose by 2 percent to $215,900, while real mean net worth rose by 7 percent to $1.24 million. Most families across the net worth and income distributions experienced increases in median and mean wealth. The homeownership rate was 66 percent in 2025, about unchanged from 2022. For families that owned a home, the median net housing value (the value of a home minus home-secured debt, such as a mortgage) rose to $230,000 in 2025 from $218,900 in 2022. Retirement plan participation, which includes account-type plans, individual retirement accounts, or defined benefit plans, was up slightly between 2022 and 2025 at around 65 percent. For families with account-type plans, mean and median balances rose. Participation in the stock market, which includes direct stock and indirect holdings, declined slightly from 58 percent in 2022 to 56 percent in 2025. Conditional on holding stock, median stock holdings grew 36 percent from $56,900 in 2022 to $77,400 in 2025. The fraction of families with any type of debt remained about stable at 77 percent. Median and mean debt outstanding remained unchanged from 2022. The fraction of families with debt payment-to-income ratios greater than 40 percent, which are families with particularly high debt payment obligations relative to their incomes, increased from 6.5 to 8.6 percent, a level last seen in the 2013 survey. In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here . Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here . The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955. Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF) Last Update:
            October 09, 2026

public_input.title: United States Department of the Treasury Announces New Appointment
public_input.body: October 9, 2026 WASHINGTON — Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent announced today a key senior appointment at the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Dr. Judy Shelton will serve as a Counselor in the Office of the Secretary. Shelton is an economist and author specializing in international financial and currency issues. She previously served as U.S. Director of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and as Chairman of the National Endowment for Democracy. She has testified numerous times before Congress as an expert witness on international financial relations and has consulted with national security officials on global economic developments. At Treasury, Shelton will advise the Secretary on currency policy, with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China. Prior to joining Treasury, Shelton served as a Senior Fellow at the Independent Institute. She also served as a Senior Research Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, where she authored The Coming Soviet Crash and Money Meltdown . She holds a Ph.D. in Business Administration from the University of Utah. Shelton began her professional career as a National Fellow at the Hoover Institution, where she received a postdoctoral fellowship to study the impact of Western capital on the Soviet economy. Throughout her career, she has specialized in analyzing the internal monetary and financial conditions of nations and their impact on exchange rates. ###

public_input.title: District of Arizona Charges 345 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week
public_input.body: Press Release District of Arizona Charges 345 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week Friday, October 9, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Oct. 3 through Oct. 9, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 345 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 151 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 172 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 21 cases against 22 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona. These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). Recent matters of interest include: United States of America v. Favela-Favela. On Oct. 5, 2026, Christina Favela-Favela was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Oct. 4, Favela drove a vehicle with her three children to the San Luis, Arizona Port of Entry seeking admission to the United States. Custom and Border Patrol (CBP) officers referred Favela’s vehicle to secondary inspection. CBP officers subsequently learned that on July 7, 2026, Favela had attempted to cross into the United States via the Lukeville, Arizona Port of Entry with two children and a male alien concealed under personal items. With this knowledge, BPAs used a canine unit on Oct. 4 and found a male passenger hiding in the fetal position under personal items in the cargo area of Favela’s vehicle. CPB officers determined the male was an illegal alien without legal authority to be in the United States. [Case Number: 26-MJ-1787] United States v. Luis Angel Diaz-Jimenez. On Oct. 5, 2026, Luis Angel Diaz-Jimenez was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien for Profit. On Oct. 2, Border Patrol Agents (BPAs) attempted to stop a Dodge Charger for an immigration inspection. Instead of yielding to BPAs, the driver, Diaz-Jimenez, accelerated, reaching speeds of approximately 100 mph before leaving the roadway, driving through a fenceline, and coming to a stop in the desert. public_input.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
public_input.body: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students Image source, BBC Indonesia Image caption, Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuse By Endang Nurdin , Rebecca Henschke , BBC Eye Investigations and BBC Indonesia Published 3 hours ago A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok. Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him , and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police. Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault Catching My Teacher Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Watch on iPlayer Listen on Sounds Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube , external . The student detectives Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar. They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school. Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school. Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations. In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said. Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent. Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions. Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name". The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases. Figure caption, Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early More students come forward The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands. One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter. "I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school." Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married , were overwhelmed by the response from former students. "It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'." Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse. "They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said. Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously. "It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC. Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process. The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time. NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals. In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward. public_input.title: US midterms: Women candidates could make history
public_input.body: Politics United States of America US midterms: Women candidates could make history Carla Bleiker 10/10/2026 October 10, 2026 The US is holding Congress and state governors elections. At all levels of US politics, women are underrepresented — but they may win some historic victories in the midterms on November 3. https://p.dw.com/p/5O695 The US is holding midterm elections on November 3 Image: Framed/Pond5 Images/IMAGO Advertisement Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women . Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women. There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers." Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades. Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do." The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa. Amy Klobuchar is already a leading Democrat in the Senate Image: Nathan Posner/Anadolu/picture alliance House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one 125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans. "There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives. The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023. Peggy Flanagan wants to become the first Native American woman to join the US Senate Image: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images/AFP US Senate: Even higher bar for women Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house. According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts. For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada. Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians. Keisha Lance Bottoms is vying to become the first ever female black governor Image: Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images/AFP First black woman state governor? Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office. For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia. Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007. But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson. This article has been translated from German. public_input.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
public_input.body: Education France French students decry failures of education system Andreas Noll 10/09/2026 October 9, 2026 For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly. https://p.dw.com/p/5O5IS University students have joined in on the protests to support schoolchildren Image: Christophe Agostinis/MAXPPP/picture alliance Advertisement Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France. At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests , young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer. Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons. The protests , which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end. France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Problems of centralization Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided. The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region. Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment. Dilapidated infrastructure Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion). According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests. France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Macron tried in vain to address problem Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success. The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created. Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray  announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation. These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now , calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally. Schoolchildren and students all over France have joined in on the protests Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS Increasing deficiencies The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example. Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days. The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it. Pupils and students in Bron, a suburb of Lyon, called for better learning conditions and investment in the education system Image: Pittore/NEIRDAPROD/SIPA/picture alliance Cancelled lessons Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers. The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts. Broken promises of equality France takes pride in its republican model of education , which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons. The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling. Students also protested against the media coverage of the problems in the education system Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance Protests in the run-up to the presidential election It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of using disproportionate force . Saint-Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko, tried to shield student protesters from riot police Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes , an allegation that the party rejects. With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle. This article was originally published in German. public_input.title: Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
public_input.body: Conflicts Eritrea Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war Philipp Sandner 10/09/2026 October 9, 2026 Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint. Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war. https://p.dw.com/p/5O3Vx ENDF patrol on October 7: The airport of Mekelle is under Ethiopian government control. But witnesses have reported Eritrean troops towards Tigray's northern border. Image: REUTERS Advertisement Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia . An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in the northenmost state of Ethiopia, Tigray. Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea have ramped up their war talk. According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory. In the letter, dated ‌Oct. 8, Ethiopian ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia left "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea," in a post on X on October 7, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Meskel had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war." Two days later, he wrote in Tigrinya, a working language of Eritrea and the main language of Tigray, that "the sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law." adding "woe to those who touch it." This comes as the regional conflict in Tigray has deteriorated rapidly in recent weeks. Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Egypt and Eritrea, causing the latter to sever diplomatic ties altogether. On Monday, when Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years as Ethiopian prime minister , he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side. Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Abiy's internal opposition: Tsimdo and the Alliance for Survival While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle , opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration. One is the Tsimdo movement, named after a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement." "The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW. It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government. The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue. The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration. "The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW. "With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now." However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo. Amhara Fano fighters (pictured here in 2021) who fought in the two-year Tigray War are part of the new Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival Image: Solan Kolli/AFP Joint declaration by Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring Sudan , Egypt , Eritrea, and Somalia . "All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said. "The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia , which is fighting the Sudanese army." In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in Somaliland . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia , which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down. Somaliland: Somalia's breakaway 'nation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively." On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued a joint declaration that didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region." And they maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states." Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise. Edited by: Benita van Eyssen Advertisement

public_input.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
public_input.body: Politics Germany Steinmeier and Macron struggle to revive Franco-German ties Rosalia Romaniec 10/09/2026 October 9, 2026 Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum. https://p.dw.com/p/5O4RX Presidents Steinmeier (l) and Macron and their wives met in Paris for a farewell Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris . The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area. Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier , his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold. It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls.  In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right. Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets.  At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris. While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt , President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace. A future, but no plan Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia . "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist. Little support for Macron's ideas Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris. A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures. Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market. How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit. As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner. It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over ; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister. The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces. The French and German Presidents took part in a ceremony in the heart of Paris Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS/dpa/picture alliance The future of defense and space On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future. It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction. As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons. Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year. Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells. This article was originally written in German. Advertisement
